summary: Ten comment-endorsed finds spanning Emacs terminals, self-hosted business software, programming books, robotics, and ancient history.
telegram_footer: 10 items surfaced | 30/30 past front-page stories processed · 3,640 comments | history + run artifact updated

items.name: Ghostel
items.summary: Libghostty-powered Emacs terminal; praised for running multiple Claude Code and Codex sessions.
items.why_included: A concrete first-hand endorsement of reliable agent sessions inside Emacs; eligible to resurface after its July appearance.
items.evidence: An Emacs user praises Ghostel's speed and reliability while running multiple Claude Code and Codex sessions.

evidence_sources.author: jwr
evidence_sources.excerpt: Thanks to libghostty and the efforts of many wonderful people, I can use ghostel in Emacs to have fast and reliable terminal emulation. I use that mostly to run multiple Claude Code and Codex sessions and it works great!

items.name: ERPNext
items.source_story_title: Running a law firm on Free software
items.summary: Open-source business suite powering a software co-op's timesheets, invoices, and accounting.
items.why_included: A real business deployment with custom automation is stronger evidence than a generic SaaS-alternative list.
items.evidence: A software co-op operator uses ERPNext for core business operations and has built modules to automate them.

evidence_sources.author: komali2
evidence_sources.excerpt: The bulk of it is run through ERPnext, which handles timesheets, invoices (client and member side), and accounting. We built some modules for ERPnext to make that as automated as possible, some of which I've finally got together this week:

items.name: Okular
items.source_story_title: Running a law firm on Free software
items.summary: KDE document viewer; a practicing lawyer praises PDF signatures and annotation features.
items.why_included: A specific professional workflow endorsement makes this more useful than a neutral PDF-reader mention.
items.evidence: A lawyer using Linux for legal work says Okular handles digital signatures well and provides annotation features.

evidence_sources.author: sombragris
evidence_sources.excerpt: For PDFs I use Okular, which handles digital signatures well and also offers a bunch of annotation features.

items.name: Writing a C Compiler
items.summary: Hands-on compiler-building book; a reader implemented the exercises in Zig and loved it.
items.why_included: A reader completed the work and explicitly found it enlightening and fun.
items.evidence: A reader worked through the book using Zig and describes the experience as enlightening and fun.

evidence_sources.author: small_model
evidence_sources.excerpt: Agree, I worked through 'Writing a C Compiler' book (I used Zig) and it was enlightening and fun.

items.name: The Little Schemer
items.summary: Scheme-based introduction to recursive thinking; a reader bought two extra copies to lend.
items.why_included: Buying additional copies to share is a particularly clear reader endorsement.
items.evidence: A reader liked The Little Schemer enough to buy two more copies specifically to lend to others.

evidence_sources.author: bigfishrunning
evidence_sources.excerpt: After reading the little schemer, I bought two more copies just to lend out to people. It's that good.

items.name: Programmers at Work
items.summary: Susan Lammers's interviews with pioneering programmers; a used-copy buyer calls it a great book.
items.why_included: Direct reader praise supports a book focused on how programmers think, not just syntax.
items.evidence: A commenter bought a used copy of Programmers at Work and calls it a great book.

evidence_sources.author: jrmg
evidence_sources.excerpt: Programmers at work: I bought a used copy of it - probably after reading this the first time it was posted. Great book, if you can find it.

items.name: Museum of Prehistoric Thera
